sermon:
A man stands in the doorway of a church he planted, and he is shaking. Not with grief. With anger. Paul has heard what they are saying in Galatia, and before he can think about pastoral warmth he writes the hardest sentence he ever wrote to a congregation. There is no thanksgiving in this letter. Every other letter opens with gratitude. This one opens with a wound.

He gets to it fast. "I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel" (Galatians 1:6). Quickly. That is the word that stings. It had not been long. The same people who wept when Paul left were now listening to teachers who told them grace was a fine start but circumcision and law-keeping would finish the job. And Paul does not call this a refinement. He calls it desertion.

**A Gospel Not Made by Men**

Paul's first move is to defend where the gospel came from, because if he received it from men, men could amend it. So he tells his story. He did not learn this message in a classroom. He did not collect it from the apostles in Jerusalem and assemble it like a syllabus. He was a persecutor, violent, advancing in Judaism beyond his peers, and then God revealed his Son in him. "I did not immediately consult with anyone," he says. Three years before he even met Peter. The gospel was not handed up the chain of human approval. It came down by revelation of Jesus Christ.

This matters because the men in Galatia were offering credentials. They were the religious experts, the ones with the heritage, the ones who could add the missing pieces. Paul says the gospel has no missing pieces. It is finished work received, not a program improved by better teachers.

**A Gospel That Cannot Be Added To**

Then comes the line that makes pastors flinch. "But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed." He says it once. Then he says it again, in case anyone thought he misspoke. Anathema. Cut off. Under the curse of God.

We need to feel how strange this is. The thing being added in Galatia was not heresy in the obvious sense. No one denied Jesus. No one renounced grace outright. They simply said grace and. Grace and the law. Grace and the ritual. Grace and your performance. And Paul names that small word and as a desertion that earns a curse, because a gospel that requires my contribution is no longer good news. It is a debt with a religious accent.

I know why this is hard to preach, because I do the same arithmetic. I believe in grace, and then I quietly grade myself by my morning routine, my discipline, my usefulness. I tell people Christ is enough and then build a private ledger where I am still trying to earn the verdict that was already given. The Galatian error is not a first-century mistake. It is the default setting of the religious heart, mine included.

**The Verdict the Curse Defends**

Why such severity over a small addition. Because of what addition does to the cross. If anything I bring completes the gospel, then Christ did not finish it, and his death was a partial payment waiting for my installments. Paul's anger is not temper. It is jealousy for the sufficiency of Jesus. The Son of God gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age. He did not deliver us so we could re-enter the age of earning under new management.

The end of the chapter is quiet after the storm. Paul, once the persecutor, is now the preacher, and the churches glorified God because of him. Grace did that. Grace took the man who tried hardest to destroy it and made him its servant. That is the whole point. Grace is not the thing we finish. It is the thing that finishes us.

So hear the warning under the anger. The most dangerous corruption of the gospel is never the loud denial. It is the small and. Watch for it in yourself.

Add to grace and lose it.

Picture a shared table. Jewish believers and Gentile believers eating together, which in the first century was not a small thing, because for centuries that table had a wall down the middle of it. And then certain men arrive from Jerusalem, and Peter, the rock, the chief apostle, the one who stood up at Pentecost, gets up and quietly moves to the other side of the room. He does not announce a doctrine. He just stops eating with the Gentiles. And Paul watches this and decides the gospel is on the line over a seating chart.

**Paul Opposed Him to His Face**

Let us not soften it. "When Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned" (Galatians 2:11). This is public. This is one apostle telling another, in front of the church, that he is wrong. Paul names the reason precisely: Peter and even Barnabas were drawn into hypocrisy. They knew the truth. Peter had eaten freely with Gentiles before the men from James showed up. His withdrawal was not conviction. It was fear of what the circumcision party would think.

And here is what Paul saw that Peter did not. By moving to the other side of the table, Peter was preaching a sermon with his feet. He was saying that to be fully accepted, the Gentile believers needed something more than Christ. They needed to become like the law-keepers. The table was not about manners. The table was about whether faith in Jesus is enough to make a person belong.

I find Peter painfully easy to understand. I have done the same thing in less obvious ways, adjusting myself to the room, signaling I belong to the respectable crowd, letting the fear of the wrong people's disapproval edit my convictions. The cowardice that bent Peter is the cowardice that bends me, and it usually wears the costume of being careful.

**Justified by Faith and Not by Works of the Law**

Then Paul lays down the sentence that the whole letter has been driving toward, the heart of the Reformation, the line that breaks every religious ledger. "A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ." He says it three times in two verses, hammering, because he wants no room for the word and. Justified. Declared righteous. The verdict of the last day spoken now, not on the basis of what I performed but on the basis of what Christ accomplished, received by faith.

This is the difference between religion and the gospel, and it is everything. One says: behave, and you may belong. The other says: you belong by faith in Christ, and now you may live. Peter's withdrawal smuggled the first message back in. Paul will not let it stand, because if acceptance runs through performance, then the cross was a gesture and not a payment.

**Then Christ Died for Nothing**

Paul presses the logic to its terrible edge. "If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose." Sit in that. If I can be set right by my obedience, then Calvary was an extravagant waste, a death no one needed. Every time I try to earn the standing I already have, I am insulting the grave I claim to trust.

And then the line where Paul stops arguing and confesses. "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me." The old Paul, the law-keeper, the persecutor, the man who had a resume, is dead. The life he lives now he lives by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him. Notice it goes personal at the very end. Loved me. Gave himself for me. Not a doctrine of justification in the abstract. A Savior with a face.

That is the table the gospel sets. There is no head and foot to it. There is no side for the respectable and a side for the rest. There is one table, one Lord, one righteousness given to all who believe, and any of us who quietly redraw the seating chart by who has performed enough is preaching against the cross with our feet.

If law could save, Christ died needlessly.

Paul has been arguing. Now he is exasperated. He opens the chapter with a question that sounds like a man holding his head in his hands. O foolish Galatians, he says, who has bewitched you. Bewitched. As if someone had cast a spell. He cannot believe a people who received the Spirit by faith would now try to finish in the flesh what only the Spirit could begin. So he asks them the plainest question available. "Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?" They know the answer. They were there. It was faith.

**Abraham Believed God**

Then Paul reaches back, far back, before Moses, before Sinai, before the law existed at all, and lands on Abraham. This is his decisive move. He quotes Genesis: Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Count the timeline. Abraham was reckoned righteous by faith centuries before the law was given. So the law cannot be the ground of righteousness, because righteousness was already being credited to a man who never kept it, never heard it, never owned a word of it. He simply believed the promise.

Which means the true children of Abraham are not those with the right bloodline or the right rituals. "It is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham." The family is a faith family. And the blessing promised to Abraham, that in him all nations would be blessed, was always aimed at the Gentiles standing in Galatia, not by their performance but by their believing. The teachers were telling these believers they were second-class until they kept the law. Paul says they were Abraham's children the moment they trusted the promise.

**The Curse the Law Could Not Lift**

But Paul will not let the law be merely unhelpful. He says it is worse than that. "All who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law." All things. Not most. The law does not offer a passing grade. It demands perfection and curses every failure, and so the man who builds his standing on law-keeping has not climbed onto a ladder. He has climbed onto a scaffold. The law is precise about this. It can tell me exactly what righteousness looks like and it has no power to make me righteous. It diagnoses. It cannot cure.

I feel the pull of the Galatian error in my own bones because performance feels safer than faith. If I can keep a list, I stay in control of the verdict. Faith means the verdict is out of my hands entirely, resting on Another, and something in me would rather carry the curse than surrender the steering wheel. That is the bewitching. It is not stupidity. It is pride dressed as devotion.

**Christ Became a Curse for Us**

Then the gospel breaks the chapter open. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree." Read it slowly. The law pronounced a curse on every lawbreaker, and rather than leave us under it, Christ went to the tree and took the curse onto himself. He did not lift the curse by lowering the law's standard. He satisfied the standard and absorbed the penalty. The cross is the law's full sentence carried out, on a substitute, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations through faith.

This is why Paul ends where he does. "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus." The dividing categories the world ranks us by, and the religious categories the false teachers ranked them by, are dissolved at the foot of the tree. If you are Christ's, you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise. Not because you performed. Because he did, and you believed.

Faith receives what works could never earn.

Paul changes the picture. He has been arguing law and faith, curse and blessing. Now he draws a family. Imagine a wealthy man's son, the heir of everything, but still a child. Legally he owns it all. Practically he is no better off than a servant. He is under guardians and managers, supervised, restricted, waiting. He has the title but not yet the freedom. That, Paul says, is what humanity was under the law: heirs in waiting, hemmed in, enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.

**When the Fullness of Time Had Come**

And then the sentence turns on a hinge of history. "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:4-5). Notice the precision. God sent his Son. Born under the law, into the very condition we were trapped in, so that he could buy us out of it. The word is redemption, a slave-market word, a price paid to set a captive free.

But Paul does not stop at freedom. Freedom from slavery could leave a man liberated and alone. The goal is not merely release. It is adoption. We were not just bought out of bondage. We were brought into a family. And to prove the family is real, God sends a second sending. He sent his Son. Then he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father. The same intimacy the eternal Son has with the Father is now breathed into us. We do not address God as a distant magistrate. We say Abba. Father.

**No Longer a Slave but a Son**

Then Paul writes a line that should undo the religious heart. "So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God." The slave works for wages, anxious, measured, always one failure from dismissal. The son does not earn his place. He has it by birth and by adoption, and the inheritance is already his name. This is the death of performance religion in a single image. A son does not lie awake wondering whether he has done enough to remain in the family. He belongs.

Which is why what comes next breaks Paul's heart. The Galatians, having been made sons, were turning back. "How can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?" Weak and worthless. The old religion of rule-keeping and calendar-watching cannot do what it promises, and yet they wanted to crawl back under it. I understand the instinct better than I would like. There is a strange comfort in slavery to rules, because rules let me measure myself and feel in control. Sonship asks me to rest, and rest can feel like falling. So I reach back for the yoke and call it discipline.

**Children of the Free Woman**

Paul closes with an unexpected illustration: Hagar and Sarah, the slave and the free, Sinai and the Jerusalem above. Ishmael was born by the flesh, by human effort to force the promise. Isaac was born by promise, by what only God could do. And Paul says, "We are not children of the slave but of the free woman." Two ways to seek God's blessing. One by the flesh, by what we can manufacture. One by promise, received as a gift. They cannot coexist. The child of the flesh persecutes the child of promise, and the slavery must be cast out.

Here is the Christ connection, and it is the center of everything. We are sons only because the Son was sent. He was born under the law so we could be born into the family. He took the position of a servant so we could take the position of heirs. The cost of our adoption was his condescension. The Spirit who cries Abba in us is the Spirit of the One who cried out, My God, my God, so that we would never have to. Stop trying to earn what he died to give you.

A son does not earn his inheritance.

Paul has won the argument. By chapter five he is no longer proving that we are free. He is telling us what to do with freedom, which turns out to be the harder question. Because there are two ways to lose your freedom, and Paul names both. You can lose it by going back under the law. And you can lose it by handing it over to the flesh. Most of us are only afraid of one of those.

**For Freedom Christ Has Set Us Free**

The chapter opens like a banner unfurled. "For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). Stand firm. The danger is real and present. The Galatians were being told that one small rite, circumcision, would complete them. Paul answers with terrible clarity: if you accept circumcision as the ground of your standing, Christ will be of no advantage to you, and you are obligated to keep the whole law. It is all or nothing. Either Christ is everything or he is nothing. You cannot keep him as a supplement.

And then Paul makes sure they understand what grace cost him personally and what it costs the proud. He says he wishes the agitators who unsettle them would go all the way with their knife logic. He is not gentle about it, because the issue is not gentle. A little leaven leavens the whole lump. A small addition does not stay small. It works through the entire loaf until the gospel of grace is gone.

**Freedom Is Not an Opening for the Flesh**

But then Paul pivots, and this is the move that keeps him from being misheard. "You were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another." There it is. Freedom is not the right to indulge myself. It is the room to love. The whole law, Paul says, is fulfilled in one word: love your neighbor as yourself. The man who thinks grace means he can finally do as he pleases has misunderstood grace as thoroughly as the man who thinks he must earn it.

So Paul gives the operative command of the Christian life: walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. Not white-knuckle the flesh into submission. Not draft a stricter rulebook. Walk by the Spirit. The flesh and the Spirit are at war within the believer, and the question is not whether you feel the war. It is which one you are walking by, step by step, moment by moment.

Then the two harvests. The works of the flesh are a sprawling, ugly list, and Paul does not blink: sexual immorality, idolatry, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, envy, drunkenness. Notice how many are sins of the heart and the temper, not just the body. I would like to think I have outgrown the gross ones, and then Paul lists jealousy and rivalry and fits of anger and I am exposed. The flesh is not just the obvious appetite. It is the resentment I nurse and the grudge I justify.

**The Fruit of the Spirit**

Against all of that, one quiet sentence. "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law." Notice it is fruit, singular, not achievements. You do not manufacture fruit by effort. Fruit grows from a living thing rooted in good soil. The Spirit produces this in those who walk by him. This is why the Christian life is neither license nor law. It is life, and life bears its own kind of fruit.

Here is the Christ connection. The flesh was crucified at the cross. "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." The same cross that justifies me also breaks the reign of my appetites, so that I am free not to obey them. Freedom is not the absence of a master. It is the right master. We were freed from the law and from the flesh for the same purpose: to love. The proof that grace has landed is not how loose I have become. It is how I serve.

Freedom serves through love, not self.

A letter written in anger ends in tenderness, and that tells you the anger was love all along. Paul has spent six chapters defending grace against those who would add to it. Now he shows what grace looks like when it lands in a room full of real people who sin and stumble and grow weary. The doctrine of free justification, it turns out, produces a particular kind of community, and you can recognize it by how it treats the fallen.

**Bear One Another's Burdens**

"Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted" (Galatians 6:1). Notice what grace does. It does not ignore the sin and it does not destroy the sinner. It restores, gently, with one eye kept honestly on its own capacity to fall. A people who know they are justified by grace and not performance have no platform from which to look down, because they did not climb up. They were carried.

"Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." There is the law again, but transformed. The law that condemned us as a ladder becomes, in Christ, the pattern of love we live by together. We carry each other. And then Paul adds, almost in the same breath, that each will have to bear his own load. There is no contradiction. We carry one another's crushing burdens, the things too heavy to lift alone, and yet each of us answers for his own walk before God. Grace makes me responsible and makes me my brother's keeper at once.

**Sowing to the Spirit or to the Flesh**

Then Paul gives the agricultural warning that should sober every one of us. "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap." This is not a denial of grace. It is the texture of a life lived under grace. The one who sows to his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh. The one who sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life. Every day I am planting something. The small, unseen choices, what I feed, what I starve, what I indulge in private, what I cultivate, are seeds, and seeds become harvests. I cannot indulge the flesh all week and expect to reap the Spirit's fruit on Sunday. The field does not lie.

So Paul says, let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap if we do not give up. There is a fatigue that comes to those who love a long time, who carry burdens that do not lift, who sow with no visible harvest. Paul does not pretend the weariness is unspiritual. He says the harvest is coming. Keep sowing.

**Boasting Only in the Cross**

And then Paul takes the pen into his own hand, writes in large letters, and ends the whole letter on the one ground he will allow a Christian to stand on. The false teachers wanted to boast in the flesh of the Galatians, to count converts and circumcisions like a scoreboard. Paul answers with the sentence that gathers the entire epistle into a single confession. "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world."

There it is. Every other ground of boasting is gone. Not my discipline, not my lineage, not my record, not my usefulness. Only the cross. And the cross does something to a man. It crucifies the world to him, so its applause and its threats lose their grip, and it crucifies him to the world, so he is dead to the game of impressing it. This is why I cannot preach this chapter from a safe distance, because I keep a quiet scoreboard too, of accomplishments and approval, and Paul calls it all flesh and points me back to the only boast that does not rot.

Neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. That is the whole letter. Not what we perform. What Christ makes. Everything in Galatians, every argument against the law, every defense of grace, every call to the Spirit, lands here: at a cross where the old self died and a new creation began, given freely, received by faith, worth more than any boast the world can offer.

Boast in the cross or boast in nothing.
